catalog_quote: There are many words in West Indian varieties of English that receive final stress as opposed to initial stress found in metropolitan varieties of English (an apostrophe before the syllable in question indicates final stress), e.g. rea'lize, cele'brate, kitchen. Sutcliffe (2003: 265) adopts the approach of Carter (1987) ... Sutcliffe views lexical tone, in the sense of distinguishing one word from another, as particularly developed in the Eastern Caribbean ... Both languages display lexical minimal pairs in common, mostly disyllables, which are differentiated by pitch patterns alone: sister (with the pitch pattern / - _ /) "female sibling", sistér (with the pitch pattern / _ - /) "a nun or sister in the religious sense"; wórker (with pitch pattern / - _ /) "one who ... pitch pattern / - /) "seamstress or needlewoman" (Sutcliffe 1982: 111). This feature has not been attested for other Caribbean creoles. Sutcliffe (2003) provides data derived from Roberts (1988: 94) for Bajan: múhda "mother, i.e. female parent", mùhdá "female head of a religious order or organization"; fáada "father, male parent ...

sweep_summary: Bajan (baja1265) is not in the catalog. The single stress-title item, Belgrave 2008 'Attitudes of Barbadians to British, American and Barbadian accents' (La Torre 13(49-50): 429-444), is a language-attitude study of national accents of standard English, not word stress: its only online traces are metadata records (Glottolog; the LangSci 302 BibTeX; a UNAM CLASE index record via CORE), and the open Mühleisen 2022 chapter (Language Science Press, p. 264) characterizes it as research on 'the acceptability of accents of standard English'. Priority none; print-only.org metadata and the Google Books feed. Best first-hand stress evidence actually read (snippets only): Blake 2008 'Bajan: phonology' (Mouton, doi:10.1515/9783110208405.1.312), section 'Stress, tone, prosody, and suprasegmentals' -- many words take final rather than initial stress (rea'lize, cele'brate), Bajan/Guyanese have disyllabic lexical minimal pairs distinguished by pitch alone (sister/sistér), CECs syllable-timed -- drawing on Sutcliffe 2003 'Eastern Caribbean suprasegmental systems' (Benjamins, doi:10.1075/veaw.g30.15sut, pp. 265-296), whose snippets state that English stress is regularly reinterpreted as high tone and that Devonish's UHT analysis applies to Bajan. Both are high-priority acquisitions (paywalled). Open items read and silent on stress: Stuka 2023, Fenigsen 2003; McClellan 1981 (lay piece) only notes 'unexpected accenting of familiar words'. Niles 1980 (Deep Blue) blocked, medium priority. Everything downloaded is under with.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is lexical and inherited from English, but a sizeable set of words carries final rather than English initial stress (rea'lize, cele'brate, kit'chen); on top of this, lexically specified pitch patterns (H-L vs L-H on disyllables: sister/sistér, múhda/mùhdá 'mother'/'mother superior', wórker) distinguish words, which Blake, following Sutcliffe 2003, treats as lexical tone. Sutcliffe's own framing (snippet) is that word stress is assigned independently of tone, so stress and pitch are separate lexical properties. No positional rule for stress is given; alternative reading if tone is set aside: lexical (unpredictable).

new_statements.exceptions: None stated beyond the general 'many words' with final stress; Wells 1982 (from Collymore 1970) adds common-noun vs. personal-name pairs ('tailor vs. Tay'lor) and noun/verb pairs ('copy vs. co'py).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms; the opening sentence is phrased for 'West Indian varieties of English' generally though it sits in the Bajan chapter. Pitch-pattern minimal pairs are Bajan-specific (data via Sutcliffe 2003 from Roberts 1988: 94). Whole passage reconstructed from overlapping Google Books snippets; 'kitchen' shows no stress apostrophe in the scanned.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Bajan/Barbadian Creole English as spoken in Barbados (baja1265, ISO bjs); Blake's opening stress sentence is phrased for West Indian English varieties in general, while the pitch-pair data are Bajan-specific (via Sutcliffe 2003 / Roberts 1988). No dialect subdivision named.

new_statements.reading: Blake states no positional stress rule for Bajan: word stress is lexical (inherited English placement) with a set of words shifted to final stress relative to metropolitan English (rea'lize, cele'brate), and, following Sutcliffe 2003, Bajan shows lexical pitch (tone-like) contrasts on disyllables (sister vs sistér), with syllable-timed rhythm. A catalog's classification would be 'lexical/unpredictable stress with lexical pitch contrasts', not a fixed-position system. Caveat: snippet-level evidence; the pitch diacritics and the mark on 'kitchen' are garbled by scanned, and the primary analysis (Sutcliffe 2003, doi:10.1075/veaw.g30.15sut) remains unread.

sources.quote: Bajan and Guyanese on the suprasegmental level is particularly obvious: both share a substantial list of lexical minimal pairs, mostly disyllables, which are differentiated by pitch patterns alone. Sister for example (with the [...] pitch pattern / - _ /) means female sibling, whereas sister (with the pitch pattern / _ - /) denotes a nun or sister [...] stress on the English stressed syllable is regularly and consistently inter[preted as] high tone, and b) many other words in Guyanese still have high tone assigned to the stressed syllable. Devonish's UHT analysis can be applied to Bajan, since we have basically the same pattern there, affecting the same words.
sources.locator: pp. 265-296 (snippet pages not shown; Blake cites p. 265 for the definition; La Torre 2006 snippet cites Sutcliffe 2003b: 280-281 for downdrift)
sources.note: The primary first-hand analysis of Bajan word prosody: English lexical stress is regularly reinterpreted as high tone (Devonish's 'underlying high tone' analysis applies to Bajan), with a set of disyllabic lexical minimal pairs distinguished by pitch pattern alone; Bajan and Guyanese 'have many more examples where significant pitch patterns (or tone) and stress part company'; rhythm described as neither syllable- nor stress-timed but 'pulse timed', with a Bajan example (8) where expected downdrift is not applied. Read only in Google Books snippets; the full chapter is the item to acquire.
